Clean, intentional shaping for hedges, ornamental shrubs, and small trees — done at the right time of year for each plant.
Cuts timed to each plant's growth cycle so re-leafing looks even
When is the best time to trim hedges in San Diego?

It varies. Most evergreen hedges respond best to a hard cut in early spring and a touch-up in mid-summer. Flowering shrubs get cut right after they bloom. We schedule each plant on its own clock, not all at once.
Can you fix a hedge that's gone too tall or hollow inside?
Often, yes — but it usually takes two or three sessions across a year, not one heavy cut. We'll walk you through the plan.

A bad trim is obvious for months. A good one disappears. We shape hedges and shrubs to look intentional from the moment we leave — never the "buzz-cut" look — and we time cuts so the plant heals into a fuller form, not a thinner one.

For larger trees or anything requiring climbing, we partner with a licensed arborist and coordinate the scheduling for you.

Can you fix just one zone, or do you need to redo the whole system?

Most of our calls are single-zone repairs — a broken head, a stuck valve, a soggy spot from a buried leak. We diagnose first and recommend a full system upgrade only when the math says it'll pay for itself.
Will a smart controller actually save me money?
For most San Diego homes, yes — typically 20–40% off the water bill. They adjust runtimes based on local weather data instead of a fixed schedule.
Do you handle SoCal Water$mart rebate paperwork?
We do. If you're replacing turf, installing drip, or upgrading to a weather-based controller, we'll prepare the submission packet.

How often should my lawn be mowed in San Diego?

Most San Diego lawns benefit from weekly service during the warm season (April–October) and every two weeks through the cooler months. We'll recommend a cadence based on your grass type, sun exposure, and irrigation.
Do you supply your own equipment?
Yes. We bring everything — commercial-grade mowers, line trimmers, blowers, fuel, and disposal. No equipment, gas, or bags to worry about.
What if it rains on my service day?
We'll reschedule to the next available day in your route. You won't be charged for a missed visit.

When should I prune my citrus trees in San Diego?
Light shaping cuts after the spring flush. Avoid heavy pruning during summer — citrus bark sunburns easily on exposed limbs in San Diego's afternoon sun.
My rose bushes look exhausted. Can they be saved?
Almost always. A proper dormant-season hard prune plus a feeding and mulch refresh in early spring brings back most roses within a single growing cycle.

Pruning is the part of landscaping where small mistakes show up months later. We prune one plant at a time, by hand, using sharp clean tools — and we know which species respond to which cuts at which time of year. It's slower than buzzing through with hedge trimmers, and the difference is visible by the next growing season.

Only as a last resort and only on hardscape joints, with the client's explicit approval. Default is mechanical removal plus mulch and pre-emergents.
Why do the same weeds keep coming back?
Most weed problems aren't a weed problem — they're a thin-mulch or bare-soil problem. A 2–3 inch mulch refresh once a year resolves 80% of recurring weed issues in beds.

Weed control isn't a single product. It's a maintenance rhythm. We combine mechanical removal, well-timed pre-emergents, and mulch depth to keep your beds clean without the constant spray-cycle you see from larger crews. If you want a fully organic program, just ask — we have an organic-only option that works in San Diego's climate.

Coastal La Jolla properties deal with salt air, slope drainage, and a unique microclimate. We've worked from Bird Rock to the village and we plan every install with those realities in mind.
Common La Jolla considerations include HOA plant lists in some neighborhoods, slope retention on hillside lots, and salt tolerance for coastal-facing properties.

La Jolla is one of San Diego's most demanding microclimates for landscaping. The marine layer keeps mornings cool and damp, then the afternoon sun hits hard — which means plant choices that work in inland neighborhoods like North Park can struggle here. We default to a salt-tolerant, sun-resilient palette for west-facing lots: agave, kangaroo paw, lavender, manzanita, and dwarf olive.

We've worked extensively in Bird Rock, La Jolla Shores, La Jolla Village, and the Muirlands. Hillside drainage is the issue that comes up most often — water that's only a nuisance on a flat lot becomes a serious erosion problem on a La Jolla slope, and most of our installs here include a regrading conversation.

Kensington's Spanish-revival homes and established hedges call for traditional, well-maintained landscapes. We specialize in restoring older formal plantings rather than replacing them.
Many Kensington properties have decades-old hedges and trees that need careful restoration, not removal. We've worked here long enough to know which mature plants are worth saving.

Kensington is one of San Diego's most architecturally consistent neighborhoods, and that translates to landscaping: there's a strong unspoken expectation that the front yard fits the era of the house. We work with that. Spanish revival lines pair beautifully with olive, lavender, and salvia. Tudor-style homes look right with formal boxwood and yew hedges. We rarely recommend tearing out mature plantings here — most of what looks tired can be brought back with two or three seasons of intentional pruning and feeding.

North Park's Craftsman bungalows and tight lot lines call for a different approach than coastal La Jolla — usually more shade, more curb-facing visibility, and more focus on character than on sweeping views.
North Park lots tend to be narrow with large mature trees, which means heavy shade, root competition, and seasonal leaf-drop driving most maintenance decisions.

The classic North Park bungalow lot is narrow, deeper than it is wide, with one or two mature trees that dominate the yard. The shade those trees throw is a gift and a constraint — most cool-season turf does fine, but warm-season Bermuda or Kikuyu will struggle. We default to a shade-tolerant Tall Fescue blend for lawns here and lean into shade-loving understory plantings like Mexican sage, hellebore, and fern for beds.

Walkability matters in North Park too: front yards are seen up close, every day, by everyone in the neighborhood. We design for that — clean edges, intentional plantings, real curb appeal — not the "pretty from the curb at 35 mph" approach that works in larger-lot neighborhoods.
